content: The Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study, also known as the Dunedin Longitudinal Study, is a comprehensive cohort study that has been ongoing for decades. It involves 1,037 individuals who were born in Dunedin, New Zealand, between April 1, 1972, and March 31, 1973. These participants were selected based on their residence in the Otago region three years after birth. The study began with an assessment of the participants at the age of three and has since conducted follow-up evaluations at ages 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 26, and most recently at age 32. Future assessments are planned for ages 38, 44, and 50. During each assessment, participants are brought back to Dunedin from wherever they reside globally. These evaluations are extensive and include interviews, physical examinations, dental assessments, blood tests, computer-based questionnaires, and surveys. Additionally, spin-off studies have been conducted, focusing on the parents of the original participants and, starting in 2007, the children of the original cohort. This approach allows for the collection of data spanning three generations within the same families. The study places a strong emphasis on participant retention, which is reflected in its remarkable success rate. At the most recent assessment at age 32, 96% of all living eligible participants (972 individuals) took part. This retention rate is extraordinary, especially when compared to the 20-40% dropout rates commonly observed in other longitudinal studies worldwide. The data collected from this study has contributed significantly to the understanding of human health and development. To date, over 1,000 academic papers, reports, book chapters, and other publications have been produced based on findings from the study. The multidisciplinary nature of the research is a key feature, with data encompassing a wide range of health domains, including: Cardiovascular health and associated risk factors Respiratory health Oral health Sexual and reproductive health Mental health Psychosocial functioning Other health areas, such as sensory, musculoskeletal, and digestive health In 1996, a book titled From Child to Adult: Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study was published to present the study's major findings in a format accessible to non-specialists. However, this book only includes data up to the age-21 assessment. Future plans for the study include publishing another book aimed at a general audience, enhancing their website to make it more user-friendly for non-specialists, and developing additional resources for public engagement. The study has also garnered significant media attention over the years. Some notable media reports include: A 2006 report on the effects of physical punishment, challenging claims of harm. A 2005 report linking cannabis use to psychotic behavior. A 2002 report on the relationship between the MAOA gene and violent behavior. A 2002 report equating the harmful effects of cannabis and tobacco. A 2001 report clearing cannabis as a direct cause of violence. The study has also resulted in numerous influential research papers. Examples include: Sex Differences in Developmental Reading Disability Psychiatric Disorders and Risky Sexual Behaviour in Young Adulthood: Cross-Sectional Study in Birth Cohort Cannabis Use in Adolescence and Risk for Adult Psychosis: Longitudinal Prospective Study Moderation of the Effect of Adolescent-Onset Cannabis Use on Adult Psychosis by a Functional Polymorphism in the Catechol-O-Methyltransferase Gene: Longitudinal Evidence of a Gene X Environment Interaction
